title: Choose a large out-of-order window despite its implementation cost
decision: Use an 80-instruction in-flight window so the processor can expose substantially more instruction-level parallelism and hide latency while maintaining a high clock speed.
rationale: The paper contrasts the 80-instruction window with the 21164's 20-instruction limit and says the larger window offers many more opportunities for parallelism; the memory system additionally tracks 32 loads and 32 stores.
outcome: The 21264 supports up to 80 instructions in partial states of completion, providing significant execution concurrency and latency hiding.
quote_as_recalled: The 21264 can accept 80, offering many more parallelism opportunities.
weakest_point: The paper clearly reports the 80-entry choice and its benefit, but does not explicitly describe the design process as a clock-frequency-versus-window-size trade study.

title: Cluster the integer register file and execution pipes into two replicated clusters
decision: Split the 80-entry integer register file into two duplicated 80-entry clusters, with two integer pipes per cluster, rather than using one fully shared four-pipe register-file structure.
rationale: A four-way integer engine would require a very large multiported register file. Clustering makes the implementation simpler and faster; the explicit cost is one extra cycle when a result must be broadcast from one cluster to the other. Dynamic issue scheduling minimizes that cost, and critical-path computations tend to remain within one cluster.
outcome: The four integer pipes are implemented as two two-pipe clusters. The paper reports only a few-percent-or-less performance difference versus an idealized unclustered implementation for most applications, while obtaining implementation simplicity, lower risk, and higher speed.
quote_as_recalled: This clustering makes the design simpler and faster, although it costs an extra cycle of latency to broadcast results from an integer cluster to the other cluster.
weakest_point: The paper does not explicitly name a single centralized four-pipe register file as the rejected design; that alternative is implicit in the clustering discussion.

title: Use line-and-way prediction to get associative-cache benefits without putting tag comparison in the critical fetch loop
where_in_paper: Instruction pipeline—Fetch / Line and way prediction, pp. 25–27
decision: Use a 64-Kbyte two-way set-associative instruction cache together with line and way prediction so the next four-instruction block can be fetched through a fast predicted path while the validity/tag check happens in parallel.
alternatives_or_rejected: A direct-mapped cache provides faster access, while ordinary set associativity improves hit rate but introduces additional access/tag-selection work; the paper explicitly presents line-and-way prediction as combining these advantages rather than selecting one of them.
rationale: The predicted line and way lets the next block be read before the full validity check completes. Decode, branch prediction, and tag comparison are kept outside the critical fetch loop. Prediction accuracy is 85% to 100% for most applications, and most mispredictions cost only one cycle.
outcome: The processor gets the higher hit rate of a 64-Kbyte two-way cache while retaining a fast fetch path; line/way mispredictions are rare and dynamically retrained.
quote_as_recalled: The processor implements a line and way prediction technique that combines the advantages of set-associative behavior and fetch bubble elimination.
weakest_point: The paper compares the technique's properties with direct-mapped and set-associative behavior, but does not present a quantified three-way design selection among cache organizations.

title: Accept one-cycle inter-cluster communication to make four-way integer issue practical
decision: Accept the latency penalty for communicating results between the two integer clusters rather than paying the implementation complexity of a fully unclustered four-way integer machine.
alternatives_or_rejected: The idealized unclustered implementation is the comparison point; the paper does not state that it was literally a candidate design rejected by the team.
rationale: The clustered organization reduces register-file and execution-network complexity and increases speed. The scheduling policy preferentially issues critical instructions on the cluster producing their operands, so the extra cross-cluster cycle usually has little effect. Simulations showed the performance cost was only a few percent or less for most applications.
outcome: The architecture combines what the authors describe as much of the implementation simplicity, lower risk, and higher speed of a two-issue machine with the performance benefits of four-way integer issue.
quote_as_recalled: The performance costs of the register clustering and issue queue arbitration simplifications are small—a few percent or less.
weakest_point: This is partly a restatement of the preceding clustering decision rather than a separately narrated design episode; the paper's explicit decision is the cluster organization itself.

title: Use speculative load-hit/miss execution with a targeted minirestart rather than restarting the whole pipeline
where_in_paper: Dynamic execution examples / Load hit/miss prediction, pp. 34–35
decision: Speculatively issue integer-load consumers early to obtain the minimum three-cycle load-hit latency, but handle a load miss with a two-cycle minirestart and then add a predictor that suppresses this speculation for loads predicted to miss.
alternatives_or_rejected: Relying on the general speculative-execution recovery mechanism would require restarting the entire instruction pipeline; the paper explicitly argues that this would be too expensive when load misses are frequent.
rationale: Consumers must issue before the cache hit/miss result is known to achieve the minimum three-cycle hit latency. A full pipeline restart after a miss is too expensive, so the processor instead squashes two integer issue cycles and pulls those instructions back into the queue. A 4-bit saturating predictor then avoids speculation when misses are predicted.
outcome: Correctly predicted hits retain the minimum three-cycle effective latency; loads predicted to miss avoid the speculative consumer issue, while an incorrectly predicted miss incurs a five-cycle effective latency rather than the cost of a full pipeline restart.
quote_as_recalled: Given that load misses can be frequent in some applications, this technique would be too expensive.
weakest_point: The final predictor is clearly described, but the paper presents the minirestart and predictor as an evolutionary response to the speculation problem rather than as one single up-front design decision.
